blocks.orig: Bagamoyo city was founded at the end of the 18th century. It is an extension of the much older settlement Kaole from the 8th century. Bagamoyo was even once the capital of German East Africa and one of the most important trading ports on the East African coast.
blocks.html: Bagamoyo was established towards the close of the 18th century as an outgrowth of Kaole, a far older settlement dating back to the 8th century. For a while the town even served as the capital of German East Africa, and it ranked among the leading harbours for commerce along the coast of East Africa.

blocks.orig: In the Kaole ruins are the remains of two mosques and 30 graves from the 13th century. Around the 17th century the settlement began to grow 2-3 miles north of Kaole. This area grew in prosperity in the 18th century. It got name Bagamoyo as an important station in the caravan trade (the name means “relief and rest”). Until the 18th century, it was a small trading centre where the majority of the population were fishermen and farmers.
blocks.html: The Kaole ruins contain what is left of two mosques and 30 graves dating from the 13th century. Around the 17th century a settlement started to develop 2-3 miles to the north of Kaole, and in the 18th century this area became prosperous. As a key stop on the caravan trade routes it received the name Bagamoyo (meaning “relief and rest”). Until the 18th century it remained a small trading centre whose inhabitants were mostly fishermen and farmers.

blocks.orig: The most important trade goods were fish, salt and rubber. In the first half of the 19th century the city became a trading port for ivory and the slave trade. Traders came from the African interior on their way to Zanzibar. This explains the meaning of the word Bagamoyo (“Bwaga-Moyo”). In Kiswahili it means “lay down your heart”. Either the name might have been given due to the slave trade that passed through the city (“give up all hope”). Or because of the porters who rested in Bagamoyo after carrying 35 pounds of cargo from the Great Lakes region on their shoulders (“unload and rest”).
blocks.html: Fish, salt and rubber were the chief commodities. In the first half of the 19th century the town became a harbour for ivory and for the slave trade, with merchants arriving from the African interior en route to Zanzibar. That history lies behind the meaning of Bagamoyo (“Bwaga-Moyo”), which in Kiswahili translates as “lay down your heart”. One explanation links the name to the slaves marched through the town (“give up all hope”); another to the porters who rested here after hauling 35 pounds of goods on their shoulders from the Great Lakes region (“unload and rest”).

blocks.orig: Many European explorers, including Richard Burton, Henry Morton Stanley and David Livingstone, began and ended their journeys here. In 1868 French missionaries founded Freedom Village in Bagamoyo as a shelter for freed slaves. For the rest of the century the town served as a stopover for missionaries travelling inland from Zanzibar. When the German Empire decided in 1905 to build a railway from Dar Es Salam to the interior, Bagamoyo’s importance began to decline and today Bagamoyo is a centre for the construction of dhow sailboats.
blocks.html: Numerous European explorers, among them Richard Burton, Henry Morton Stanley and David Livingstone, started and finished their expeditions in Bagamoyo. In 1868 French missionaries set up Freedom Village here as a refuge for freed slaves, and for the remainder of the century the town was a stopover for missionaries heading inland from Zanzibar. Once the German Empire decided in 1905 to lay a railway from Dar Es Salam into the interior, Bagamoyo’s significance started to fade. Today the town is a centre for building dhow sailing boats.

blocks.orig: The government is working to preserve the colonial ruins in and around Bagamoyo and to revive the city. Bagamoyo’s tranquil pace and fascinating history make it a pleasant day or weekend trip.
blocks.html: The government is making efforts to protect the colonial ruins in and around Bagamoyo and to bring the town back to life. With its relaxed pace and rich history, Bagamoyo makes for an enjoyable day trip or weekend away.

blocks.orig: The best time to visit is between the months of June through October because this is the dry season when rainfall is almost non-existent. At this time, the skies are clear and the waters of the sea are a stunning sapphire blue with contrasting azure. The annual highlight is the Bagamoyo Arts Festival, usually held around late September or October.
blocks.html: June through October is the best period for a visit, as this is the dry season and there is hardly any rain. The skies are clear then and the sea is a striking sapphire blue set against azure. The highlight of the year is the Bagamoyo Arts Festival, which normally takes place in late September or October.

blocks.orig: Travel Tips from our experts about Bagamoyo

My name is Hassan and I am a guide in Bagamoyo for 13 years. Our guests come here mainly because the area is full of Tanzania’s history. They feel like walking in a long gone era when Sultans ruled the country and slaves were sold and shipped to foreign places.
blocks.html: I am Hassan, and I have been a guide in Bagamoyo for 13 years. Most of our guests come because the area is steeped in Tanzania’s history. It feels like stepping back into a vanished age, when Sultans ruled the country and slaves were sold and shipped abroad.

blocks.orig: Bagamoyo city is an old settlement and was once one of the most important trading ports on the East African coast. Trade goods were first fish, salt and rubber and in the first half of the 19th century for ivory and the slaves. The Kaole ruins nearby are the remains of two mosques and 30 graves from the 13th century.
blocks.html: The old settlement of Bagamoyo was at one time a leading harbour for commerce along the coast of East Africa. Early on, fish, salt and rubber changed hands here; during the first half of the 19th century ivory and slaves followed. Close by, the Kaole ruins preserve what is left of two mosques and 30 graves dating back to the 13th century.
